purpose: Converts electrical signals into audible sound waves and acoustic tones. Essential for providing instant auditory feedback, security alarms, timer countdowns, and system health status beeps on standalone IoT projects without requiring an attached screen.

whenToUse.scenario: Active Buzzer for Instant Alarms & Beeps (Simple HIGH/LOW)
whenToUse.why: When you only need a clear, loud single-frequency warning beep (e.g. burglar alarm, microwave timer, door chime). Contains its own built-in oscillator; apply 5V and it sounds immediately.
whenToUse.recommended: 5V Active Buzzer (sealed top sticker with '+' mark)

whenToUse.scenario: Passive Buzzer for Musical Melodies & Multi-Frequency Tones
whenToUse.why: When you want to play custom tunes (like the Super Mario theme or 8-bit game effects) or generate varying pitch tones based on sensor distance. Has no internal oscillator; you supply the frequency via Arduino's tone() function.
whenToUse.recommended: 5V Passive Piezo Buzzer (green bottom PCB, exposed coil)

whenToUse.why: Short, crisp 20ms clicks confirm button presses, RFID card badge swipes, or keypad entries so the user knows their input was registered.
whenToUse.recommended: Passive Piezo Buzzer with 100Ω current limiting resistor

whenToUse.scenario: Loud Industrial & Outdoor Sirens (12V High Decibel)
whenToUse.why: When a small 85dB breadboard buzzer is too quiet for a large room or noisy workshop. Driven by an external 12V power supply through an NPN transistor or MOSFET switch.
whenToUse.recommended: 12V 110dB Piezo Alarm Siren driven by 2N2222 or IRLZ44N

basics.title: The Golden Rule: Active vs Passive
basics.text: Active Buzzers have an internal oscillating circuit inside the black housing: simply write digitalWrite(pin, HIGH) and it beeps. Passive Buzzers have no internal circuit: writing HIGH makes only a tiny click! You MUST send an alternating AC frequency using tone(pin, 440) to vibrate the diaphragm.

basics.title: How to tell them apart visually
basics.text: Look at the underside: Active buzzers have their bottom sealed with black potted epoxy. Passive buzzers typically have an exposed green circuit board with visible solder traces. Also, active buzzers usually come with a removable peel-off paper label on top.

basics.title: Pin Current & Protection
basics.text: A standard piezo element draws only 10–20mA, which is safe for an Arduino Nano pin directly. However, electromagnetic buzzers can pull 50mA+ and kick back inductive voltage when switching off; always use an NPN transistor (2N2222) and a 1N4148 flyback diode for large buzzers!

types.name: Active Piezo Buzzer
types.summary: Self-oscillating acoustic transducer. Produces a loud ~2.3 kHz fixed tone as soon as DC voltage (3.3V–5V) is applied.
types.applications: Burglar alarms, countdown timers, warning indicators

types.name: Passive Piezo Buzzer
types.summary: Pure speaker diaphragm. Requires an external square wave frequency (PWM) from the microcontroller to create sound. Can play any musical note from 31 Hz to 65,535 Hz.
types.applications: Melody players, frequency sounders, variable-pitch distance feedback

types.name: Electromagnetic Buzzer
types.summary: Uses a tiny magnetic coil to vibrate a ferromagnetic metal disc. Offers deeper bass tones at lower frequencies, but draws more current (30–80mA).
types.applications: Automotive dashboard chime, appliance feedback, computer motherboards

examples.title: Playing Tones & Notes with a Passive Buzzer
examples.description: Generate musical frequencies on pin D8 using the built-in Arduino tone() library.
